1: The serpent enters the scene as one of God’s creatures.
The story says the serpent was especially crafty.
That craftiness is set beside the other animals.
The phrase means every creature in the field group.
The serpent is compared with all the field animals.
These are the wild creatures of the open country.
The verse ties the comparison to what God made.
God formed these creatures too.
The LORD is named as their maker.
God’s name appears with the LORD’s.
Now the serpent begins to speak.
It directs its words to the woman.
The woman is the one it addresses.
The question opens with a sharp “Really?”—the serpent challenges what God said.
This little word introduces the claim being questioned.
The serpent repeats God’s words back to her.
God is the one whose command is under discussion.
It makes the command sound like a ban.
Eating is the action the serpent puts in doubt.
The question sweeps in every tree.
The tree is what the serpent says God forbade.
It frames the whole garden as off-limits.
2: The woman answers with her own words.
Her answer is directed to the serpent.
She names the serpent she is answering.
The fruit is what God allowed them to eat.
The garden’s trees provide the fruit.
The garden is the setting of God’s generous permission.
The woman says they may eat.
3: She adds that fruit is also part of the answer.
The fruit comes from the tree she is about to name.
This word connects the tree to the earlier thought.
The tree stands in the garden’s middle.
That is the garden God planted.
She says this is what God spoke.
God is the one who gave the command.
The boundary is stated as a clear “no.”
Eating is the act they must not do.
The command concerns eating from that tree.
She repeats the prohibition with added emphasis.
Touching is the extra boundary she mentions.
The prohibition is aimed at the tree itself.
This word introduces the danger of what could happen.
The warning is that they could die.
4: The serpent is the one contradicting the warning.
It speaks directly to the woman.
The woman hears the lie face to face.
Death is what God warned would follow.
The serpent repeats the warning only to deny it.
5: The serpent gives its reason for the lie.
It claims God knows something the woman does not.
God is the one whose knowledge it invokes.
This word introduces the serpent’s claim.
The day of eating is what it names.
Eating is the choice it points to.
The fruit is what the serpent says they will eat.
It says their eyes will be opened.
Their eyes are the part it says will change.
It promises they will become something more.
They will know, the serpent says.
The word good is paired with evil.
Evil completes the pair it names.
6: The woman looks closely at the tree.
She is the one weighing what she sees.
This word introduces what she decides about it.
The tree looks good to her.
The tree’s fruit is in view.
It appears good for eating.
She adds another reason to her judgment.
Desire rises as she looks at it.
The tree is the object of that desire.
Its fruit looks pleasing to her eyes.
The tree itself now seems desirable.
The tree remains the focus of her gaze.
She believes it can make one wise.
Then she reaches out and takes the fruit.
It is the fruit she takes for herself.
She eats it.
Then she gives some to another.
The man receives some too.
She gives it to her husband.
He is there beside her.
He eats as well.
7: Their eyes open after they eat.
The eyes of both are named.
Neither of them is left out of this moment.
Now they know what has changed.
This word introduces their new awareness.
They use leaves from a tree.
The fig tree supplies the covering.
They make coverings for their bodies.
These are makeshift belts or aprons.
8: They hear the sound of God in the garden.
This marks the voice they hear.
The LORD is the one coming near.
God is named with the LORD.
He is walking through the garden.
The garden is the place where they hear Him.
The breeze of the day is mentioned.
It is the day’s cool part.
The man and woman hide themselves.
The LORD is the one they avoid.
The trees become their hiding place.
They hide within the garden itself.
9: The LORD is the one who calls.
The one who calls is God Himself.
His call is directed toward the man.
The man is the one God seeks an answer from.
The question is addressed to him.
10: The voice he heard is named.
He heard God in the garden.
He explains what made him afraid.
The man is speaking about himself.
11: God asks the man a question.
Someone, the man is asked, told him this.
God returns to what the man says about being naked.
The man says he is naked.
The question turns back to the tree.
This is the tree God forbade.
The command came through God’s own word.
God reminds him He gave the command.
The boundary was clear: do not.
The man was not to eat from it.
This points back to the tree.
God asks plainly: did you eat?
12: The man answers, but begins by naming someone else.
He is the one God questioned.
He describes her as the one connected to his story.
He says God gave her to him.
He says she was with him.
The woman is who he blames.
He says she gave the fruit.
He says she gave it to him.
The fruit came from the tree.
13: God turns to the woman and speaks.
The LORD is the one asking.
God is named as judge and listener.
He directs His question to the woman.
He asks what she has done.
This one—the action—is brought into view.
She also admits that she ate.
14: God speaks judgment over the serpent.
The LORD is named as judge.
God’s name appears again.
His words are directed to the serpent.
The serpent is now confronted.
God names the reason for judgment.
The serpent did this.
The act is pointed out: what you did.
The serpent is cursed.
God speaks to it directly.
Its curse is set over the creatures around it.
Even the livestock are included in the comparison.
The word widens the list to every creature.
The wild animals are named.
The field is their setting.
The serpent will crawl low.
Its belly touches the ground.
That is how it will go.
Dust is named as its food.
It will eat dust.
This judgment lasts through all its days.
The days of its life are in view.
Its life is marked by this humbling.
15: God declares hostility between the serpent and the woman.
He sets this enmity in place.
And it will reach between their offspring too.
The woman’s descendants are in view.
The conflict reaches the serpent’s offspring.
The woman’s offspring is named again.
He is the one who will strike the serpent.
The serpent’s head is the target.
The head is where the blow lands.
It will wound the man’s heel.
The heel is where the wound falls.
16: The increase is repeated for emphasis.
Her sorrow and toil will grow.
Pregnancy is part of the pain described.
She will give birth in pain.
The verse then turns toward her husband.
Her husband is the man beside her.
He, the husband, is also in view.
The verse describes the struggle now entering their relationship.
17: God addresses Adam.
Adam is the one who must answer.
This gives the reason for the judgment.
He listened to his wife’s voice.
Her voice is what he followed.
The woman is named as his wife.
He ate from the tree.
The fruit came from it.
This is the tree they were warned about.
God had spoken this command to him.
The command came directly from God.
He told him exactly what to do.
The command was “do not.”
Adam was not to eat.
That tree was off-limits.
Now the ground is cursed.
The soil is the ground under the curse.
This hardship comes because of Adam.
Painful work will mark his days.
He will eat from the ground through toil.
The work stretches across all his days.
The days of his life are in view.
His life will carry this burden.
18: The land will sprout them for him.
They will come up where he works.
He will still eat from the field.
The food is what he must gather.
The field is where he will find them.
19: Sweat will mark the work of his face.
He will earn food by working.
Bread is the food he needs.
This hardship lasts until a day comes.
He will return to the ground.
The soil is where he will go.
The ground is where he began.
This gives the reason for his return.
He was taken from the ground.
God speaks directly to him: you.
He will return to the dust.
The dust is the end of this earthly life.
He will go back to it.
20: The man gives his wife a name.
Adam is the one naming her.
This explains why he chooses that name.
She is the mother of all living.
Her children will be born into the human story.
Every living person comes into view.
Life is carried forward through her.
21: God makes clothing for the couple.
The LORD is the one who provides it.
God’s name stands with this act of care.
He makes clothing for the man.
The garments are made from skin.
22: God speaks about what the man has become.
The LORD is the speaker.
God names the situation.
“Look,” He says.
The man is the one in view.
He has become like one of us.
This comparison is to one.
It is one among us.
The man now knows good and evil.
This is the good side of what he now knows.
Evil is the other side.
Now God speaks of what comes next.
This means “lest” or “so that not.”
The man might reach out his hand.
His hand is what could take the fruit.
He might take from the tree.
He might take that too.
This is the tree of life.
Life is what the tree offers.
He could eat from it.
Then he would live.
The life would go on forever.
23: God sends the man away from the garden.
The LORD is the one who sends him.
He sends him out from Eden’s garden.
Eden is the garden he leaves.
The man is sent to work.
The soil is what he must tend.
This is the ground he came from.
The verse points back to that ground.
Now he is sent away from there.
24: The man is the one expelled.
He leaves the garden’s life behind.
God stations guardians at the east of Eden.
Eden is where the garden stands.
And the flame is named too.
Its task is to guard the path.
The way to the tree is kept safe.
This is the path they once walked.
The tree of life is the guarded destination.
Life is what the tree represents here.
